title: Partial types (splitting one type across files)
hook: The `partial` keyword lets one type live in multiple files. Source generators write one part; you write another — without merge conflicts or duplicate type names.

blocks.text: A **partial type** is a class, struct, interface, or record split across multiple source files. Every part uses the `partial` keyword and shares the same type name and namespace. The compiler merges them into one type. This is the standard pattern for **source generators** — tools that emit code at compile time.

entries.plainDefinition: A keyword that marks one piece of a type definition. All parts compile into a single type.
entries.example: `public partial class CsvWorker { ... }` in two files.

entries.plainDefinition: A compile-time tool that reads your code and emits additional C# files. Often uses `partial` types.
entries.example: A generator that creates CSV column-mapping code from attributes.

entries.plainDefinition: A method split between a declaration (often in generated code) and an implementation (in your code).
entries.example: `partial void OnRowParsed(string row);` — you implement it; generator calls it.

entries.plainDefinition: A constructor split between a defining declaration and an implementing body in different files.
entries.example: Generator declares `public partial CsvWorker(string path);` — you write the body.

blocks.text: Without `partial`, a source generator would have to rewrite your entire file on every build — wiping your hand-written logic. Partial types let the generator own its slice while you own yours. C# 14 extended `partial` to constructors and events, so generators can declare surfaces and you wire the implementation.

blocks.title: Combine with file-local types
blocks.body: Generators often pair `file`-local helper types (access modifiers topic) with `partial` public types. Consumers see one public worker; helpers stay invisible outside the file.

items.title: Every part must say `partial`
items.body: All files declaring the same type use `partial class`, `partial struct`, etc.

items.title: One primary constructor across all parts
items.body: C# 14: only one part may declare a primary constructor. Other parts use ordinary or partial constructors.

items.title: Partial constructor: one definer, one implementer
items.body: The defining part declares the signature. The implementing part provides the body. Only the implementer may use `this()` or `base()`.

items.title: Partial events (C# 14)
items.body: The defining part looks field-like. The implementing part supplies `add` and `remove` accessors.

snippet.label: Partial constructor split (C# 14)
snippet.explanation: Line 3: generated file declares the constructor signature. Line 10: your file implements it with validation. One type, two files, no merge conflicts.

snippet.label: Partial method — generator calls, you implement
snippet.explanation: Line 4: generated code declares and calls `OnMapped`. Line 15: you provide the implementation. If you omit the body, the call is erased (for void partial methods without a body requirement).

snippet.label: Partial event (C# 14)
snippet.explanation: Line 3: generated file declares the event surface. Line 9: your file wires `add`/`remove`. Delegates and events in depth are module 10.

blocks.title: Partial types in C# vs JS/TS
rows: JS modules and composition — no language-level partial class
N/A — all parts must agree on `partial`
TS interface merging is type-space only, not runtime
Source generators emit `partial` files at compile time
Build tools generate JS/TS files — no `partial` keyword
No equivalent — one constructor per class

blocks.title: Two primary constructors in different parts
blocks.body: C# 14 allows only one primary constructor across all partial parts. Putting `class Foo(int x)` in two files is a compile error.

blocks.title: Business logic in the generated file
blocks.body: The next `dotnet build` will overwrite generated code. Keep your logic in the hand-written partial file.

interviewTakeaways: `partial` is one type across multiple files — the generator pattern.
C# 14: partial constructors and partial events, one implementer each.
Only one part may use primary constructor syntax.
commonPitfalls: Two primary constructors in different parts.
Putting business logic in the generated file so the next generate wipes it.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript interface merging is a type-space feature. C# `partial` is one runtime type built from several syntactic parts.
JavaScript classes are one declaration (or a runtime mixin). Splitting implementation is modules and composition, not a language-level partial type.
